value.overview: The White-tipped Dove is a medium-sized tropical dove found from southern Texas and Mexico through Central and South America. It is usually secretive, spending much of its time walking on the ground beneath trees and shrubs. Its soft, repeated calls are often easier to detect than the bird itself. The species tolerates a range of wooded environments and is a familiar resident of many lowland and foothill habitats in Costa Rica.
value.classification: The White-tipped Dove belongs to the dove and pigeon family Columbidae. It is one of several ground-feeding doves in the genus Leptotila.
value.identification: This dove is about 27 centimeters long, with a warm gray-brown back, a gray head, and a pinkish or vinaceous chest. The neck and upper breast may show subtle green or purple iridescence. Its most distinctive feature is the white outer tail feathers, visible when the tail is spread or the bird flies. It has a slender dark bill, reddish legs, and a relatively long, rounded tail. It is generally less boldly marked than related quail-doves.
value.rangeHabitat: The White-tipped Dove ranges from southern Texas and Mexico south through Central America to much of South America. In Costa Rica it is a common to abundant resident, especially in the lowlands along the Pacific slope. It also occurs in suitable foothill habitats, reaching roughly 800 meters in northern mountain areas and about 1,500 meters or higher in parts of central and southern Costa Rica. Habitats include forest edges, secondary woodland, plantations, gardens, scrub, and other areas with dense ground cover.
value.migrationStatus: The White-tipped Dove is generally resident and does not undertake regular long-distance migration. In Costa Rica it is present throughout the year, although local movements may occur as birds respond to food availability, rainfall, and habitat conditions.
value.breeding: Breeding may occur during different parts of the year across its broad range, often coinciding with favorable rainfall and food conditions. The nest is a simple, loosely built platform of twigs placed in a shrub, small tree, or other vegetation. The clutch usually contains two white eggs. Both parents participate in incubation and care of the young. In Costa Rica, breeding can occur in lowland and foothill woodland, forest margins, plantations, and well-vegetated gardens.
value.dietFeeding: The White-tipped Dove feeds mainly on seeds, fallen fruits, berries, and other plant material collected on or near the ground. It may also take small quantities of invertebrate food. The bird commonly forages alone or in pairs beneath trees, along forest paths, and at woodland edges, using its bill to search through leaf litter and low vegetation. It often visits areas where fruiting plants or spilled grain provide concentrated food.
value.behavior: This dove is usually quiet and cautious, walking slowly through shaded vegetation and remaining difficult to see. When disturbed, it may flush suddenly with rapid wingbeats and reveal its white-tipped tail. Its low, rhythmic call is frequently heard from dense cover, particularly in the early morning. White-tipped Doves are commonly solitary or found in pairs, although several may gather where food is abundant. They often use the same sheltered feeding areas repeatedly.

conservation.populationTrend: No major global decline is currently recognized for the species.
